question: A standard commercial eye drop (approximately 50 μL) exceeds the conjunctival sac capacity of 7–10 μL, meaning the excess drug is primarily lost via nasolacrimal drainage into the systemic circulation.

l10n.wrongAnswerMessage: This is TRUE. This is the pharmacokinetic basis for nasolacrimal occlusion (NLO) counselling: pressing the lacrimal sac area for 1–2 minutes after instillation reduces systemic absorption by up to 50%, which is clinically important for drugs like timolol (bradycardia, bronchospasm) and brimonidine (systemic hypotension).
l10n.correctAnswerMessage: Correct. The conjunctival sac can hold only 7–10 μL of fluid comfortably (maximum ~30 μL with forced retention). A standard 50 μL drop deposits 5× the useful capacity. The overflow drains via the nasolacrimal duct into the nasal mucosa, where rapid systemic absorption occurs — explaining topical beta-blocker (timolol) cardiovascular side-effects.
